title: The Hajj of the heart
hook: those who can't go share in it by fasting Arafah and by longing

segments.voice: Yesterday, visiting Medina, and your line: peace on you, messenger. When his name came up, did you pause and send peace? Day one thousand one hundred forty.

They came asking for something to ride. An expedition was setting out, and these men wanted to go, but they had no mount and no money for one. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told them he had nothing to carry them on. Surah At-Tawbah keeps what happened next. They turned away with their eyes overflowing with tears, grieving that they couldn't find the means. The Qur'an says there is no blame on them. They stayed home. Their tears went on the record anyway. Today, the Hajj of the heart.
screen: `NOTHING TO RIDE.` → `EYES OVERFLOWING.` → `NO BLAME ON THEM.`

segments.voice: This path began the pilgrimage with a condition: the Hajj is due on those who can find a way. Since then, the lessons have followed people who could. Today is for everyone else. First, the men in tears. The verse in Surah At-Tawbah doesn't scold them for staying home. It names their grief and lifts the blame. Wanting to go and being unable is a different thing from not wanting to go. Second, the people left behind. Anas reports, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that on the way home from that expedition the Prophet told his companions: there are people in Medina who were with you on every road you traveled and every valley you crossed. They were held back by an excuse. Held back, and still with you. Third, a rule of thumb from the same collection. When a servant of God falls ill or travels, the Prophet said, the good he used to do while healthy and at home is still written for him. The record follows the person's habit and intention, not just their location. Fourth, what people at home actually do. On the day of Arafah, while the pilgrims stand on the plain, Muslims who aren't there are encouraged to fast, and Sahih Muslim records the Prophet's praise for that fast. And in the first days of Dhul Hijjah, a person who plans to offer a sacrifice is told, in another report in Muslim, to leave their hair and nails uncut until it's done, a small echo of the pilgrim's restraint, kept at home, far from Mecca. So on the day of Arafah, while the plain fills, someone in an ordinary kitchen keeps the fast, and that is their share of the day.
screen: `IF THEY CAN FIND A WAY.` · `TEARS, AND NO BLAME.` · `HELD BACK, AND STILL WITH YOU.` · `FASTING ARAFAH FROM HOME.` · then, large: `THEY WERE HELD BACK BY AN EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: long for it. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can ask God, in your own words, for the chance to go one day, or for the chance for someone you love to go. Ask plainly, the way the men who came asking for a mount asked. If you don't pray, think of a place you've always wanted to stand in, and couldn't yet. Let yourself want it, without hurrying the wanting away. Notice where you feel it. The bell holds the time.
The Hajj of the heart. Taking part from home, by longing, by fasting on the day of Arafah, and by the intention of those who are held back by an excuse. Today's word.
screen: `THE HAJJ OF THE HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: longing counts. Today, name one good thing you can't do yet, and do one small piece of it from where you are. Tomorrow: five pillars, one house. Day one thousand one hundred forty.

howItsDone: Muslims who cannot make the pilgrimage may fast on the day of Arafah, say the takbir through the first days of Dhul Hijjah, offer a sacrifice at Eid al-Adha if able, and ask God for the chance to go.

fork.setup: you came to the Prophet asking for a mount so you could go. he tells you he has none to give you. what happens next, by the Qur'an's telling?
options: they turn away in tears, and there is no blame on them.
they set out on foot anyway.

trapdoor: what you thought: wishing you were on Hajj.
what it means: taking part from home, by fasting Arafah, by restraint, and by longing.
what a scholar hears: Anas's report in Bukhari: held back by an excuse, and still with you on every road.

notes: 9:92 is paraphrased (the men who came asking for mounts and turned away weeping). Commentators connect it to the Tabuk expedition; the script says only 'an expedition'.
Bukhari 2839 (also 4423, Anas, returning from Tabuk): 'people in Medina... held back by an excuse'. Confirm number.
Bukhari 2996 (Abu Musa): the ill and the traveler credited with what they used to do. Confirm.
Muslim 1162: the fast of Arafah; the expiation of two years is deliberately not stated here (taught on day 1114).
Muslim 1977: one intending to sacrifice leaves hair and nails from the start of Dhul Hijjah. Schools differ on whether this is obligatory or recommended; confirm phrasing 'is told'.
Practice invites asking 'in your own words' if you pray; no new prayer written.

Editor: fixed the garbled 'restraint... kept in a kitchen' (hair and nails left uncut at home); replaced the closing uplift ('isn't a consolation prize') with a concrete image of the Arafah fast at home.
